title: Methodology & Measurement
subtitle: How every reading on this map is taken, where its source of truth sits, and what it cannot see. The map makes an argument, so the method behind it is documented in full: anyone should be able to rerun it and get the same record.

principles.p: Level 1 is taken from the public record. DNS is read the way any mail server reads it. Each public website is visited once, the way a browser visits it, to read one response header and one public file (/.well-known/security.txt). No login is attempted, no port is probed, no vulnerability is exercised, and no traffic is sent to any look-alike domain. Level 2 is the cooperative inspection, where the organization opens the door and shows evidence.

Each control is recorded as pass, below code, advisable, or not observable against a single named requirement. There is no composite score and no ranking. No organization is called good or bad; a specific, checkable fact is placed on the record, dated and sourced.

principles.h: A matter of record, not a finding
principles.p: An appearance on a screening list or a ransomware leak site is reported as a matter of public record: dated, linked to its source, and read in context. A leak-site listing is an attacker's claim. An export-control listing is not a sanction. Neither is a finding of wrongdoing by anyone.

Where a signal cannot be resolved (a DKIM key on an uncommon selector, a DNS answer too large for the resolver path, a website that refused the read, name servers that answered inconsistently) it is recorded as not observable, never as a failure. The instrument states what it could see, not what it assumes.

The one observable Floor control costs close to nothing: an enforcing DMARC record is a single line of DNS. Cheaper Standard-Practice signals cost as little — a security.txt is one text file — but they sit above the Floor, not on it. The Floor is the same for a trillion-dollar lab and a ten-person nonprofit, because the model access a lab hands to either is the same. Where an organization lives on a parent's domain (a ministry, a university), the record names the parent and says so.

population.rule: An organization is on this map because it put its own name to a written commitment or warning about AI risk or security, or because a frontier lab's own published document records entrusting it with model access. The author did not choose who matters. Every profile links the document that put the organization here and quotes it.
rings: Named in a frontier lab's own system card as an external evaluator or red team (Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind system cards, 2024 to 2026).

Signatories of the Frontier AI Safety Commitments (AI Seoul Summit, May 2024, with later additions): the pledge includes investing in cybersecurity and insider-threat safeguards for unreleased model weights.
Organizations that published, under their own name, a warning of catastrophic or extinction-level AI risk, or a rating of the labs' safety practices.
Members of the international network of government AI safety institutes, beyond the two already listed as evaluators.

AI developers and security-ratings firms among the 666 signatories of the Collective Cyber Defense letter (27 August 2026), whose first ask of every organization is to fix its highest-risk weaknesses.
population.verification: Every inclusion document was fetched and the quoted sentence read back from it. Where the text available showed only a heading or a co-authored paper, the organization was held back rather than included on a weak reading; the held list and the reason for each is published below.

coverage: 65 organizations across five rings. Every one carries the Level 1 read: DNS from public resolvers; one HTTP read of each public website, paced, one visit per site; passive exposure data from Shodan InternetDB; the FireHOL level1 blocklist; the US Consolidated Screening List; and ransomware.live's public victim search. Every one also carries a linked inclusion source. The curb read is necessary, not sufficient: it says nothing about the controls that protect model weights from a state-level attacker, which sit behind Level 2 and beyond it.

signals.name: DMARC policy
signals.source: RFC 9989 (DMARC), which obsoletes RFC 7489 and RFC 9091
signals.what: Whether the domain's published DMARC record requests that receiving mail servers reject or quarantine a message forged in its exact name (p=quarantine or p=reject), expresses no preference (p=none), or is absent.
signals.measure: Three things are kept distinct. (1) The DNS record observed: the _dmarc TXT record as published. (2) The policy it requests: p=reject or p=quarantine is read as requesting enforcement and clears the observable Floor; p=none, or no record, requests no enforcement. Per RFC 9989 the pct tag is retired and the t tag (t=y) marks a testing posture; a record still carrying pct<100 is read as an enforcing policy in partial rollout — it clears the Floor with that caveat shown on the profile, and is never described as a specific rejection percentage. (3) Actual receiver behaviour is NOT measured: what any given receiver does with failing mail is its own local policy, receivers do not all follow the same standard, and this inspection reads only the published record. p=none does not guarantee delivery, and p=quarantine is not rejection.
signals.limit: DMARC governs only the organization's own exact domain; it does nothing against a look-alike domain or a compromised legitimate mailbox. The record states a request, not an outcome — no claim is made about whether forged mail is actually rejected. It is the one Floor control observable from the curb; the rest of the Floor is a Level 2 determination.

signals.name: SPF
signals.what: Whether unauthorised senders of the domain's mail are rejected.
signals.measure: The domain's TXT records are read for v=spf1 and the terminal mechanism classified: -all, ~all, ?all/+all.
signals.limit: Many large domains publish TXT sets too large for the UDP path this scan could use; those are recorded as not observable. The scheduled scan, which can fall back to TCP, fills them.

signals.name: DKIM key presence
signals.what: Whether the domain publishes a key to sign its outbound mail.
signals.measure: Twenty-five common selectors are queried at selector._domainkey, following CNAMEs, for a published key.
signals.limit: This establishes only that a key is published at a common selector. It does not establish that outbound mail is actually signed, nor that the signature aligns with the From domain. A domain using an uncommon or private selector is recorded as not observable, never as an absence of DKIM.

signals.name: MTA-STS record
signals.what: Whether inbound mail is protected against silent downgrade, with failures reported.
signals.measure: The _mta-sts TXT record is read for a valid v=STSv1 declaration.
signals.limit: Only the DNS record is read. The policy file itself, and whether it is in enforce or testing mode, are not fetched, so this is the presence of an advertised policy, not proof of an enforced one.

signals.name: Look-alike domains
signals.what: Whether a mail-capable homoglyph or one-keystroke typo of the domain is registered.
signals.measure: Homoglyph and one-keystroke variants of the domain are generated and each checked for registration and mail-capable records. Registrations by the organization itself are counted separately as defensive.
signals.limit: A registered look-alike is an observation, not a finding of malicious intent: many belong to unrelated businesses, and shared commodity name servers or mail providers do not establish common ownership. An organization also cannot control what third parties register. The generated variant set is heuristic, not exhaustive.

signals.name: HSTS
signals.what: Whether the public website tells browsers never to fall back to plain HTTP.
signals.measure: One same-origin GET of the homepage in an ordinary browser; the Strict-Transport-Security header is read. A max-age of six months or more meets the control; a shorter one is recorded as short.
signals.limit: Reads the host the apex redirected to. A site behind a bot challenge that refuses the read is not observable.

signals.name: security.txt
signals.what: Whether the organization publishes where to report a vulnerability in it.
signals.measure: One same-origin GET of /.well-known/security.txt; the file counts when it is served as text, carries a Contact field, and its Expires date is in the future. An expired file is recorded as expired.
signals.limit: An organization may run a disclosure page or bug bounty without a security.txt; that is not detected, which is why F5 sits at Standard Practice in this edition rather than on the Floor.

signals.name: Web-host exposure (assessed host)
signals.what: What a single passive read of the one web host the domain resolves to shows about which ports answer on that address.
signals.measure: The single address the website resolves to is looked up in Shodan's passive InternetDB. A host on which only web ports (HTTP/HTTPS) answered is recorded as a scoped observation that only web ports answered on that one address; this is not a determination that a CDN, WAF or other protective infrastructure is in place, and it is not a read of the whole infrastructure. A host that also answers non-web services (remote administration, file transfer, a database) is recorded as such, with which services, and any indexed vulnerabilities, held to Level 2.
signals.limit: This is a passive read of one assessed host, not a scan and not a statement about the organization's wider infrastructure. 'Only web ports' on that host is not proof of a protective CDN or WAF, and says nothing about other addresses the organization operates.

signals.name: Known-exploited services
signals.what: Whether directly reachable services carry known-exploited vulnerabilities.
signals.measure: A Level 2 determination. Establishing that no directly-reachable service across the organization's infrastructure carries a known-exploited or critical CVE requires more than a passive read of one public web host.
signals.limit: Held to Level 2. A single passive web-host observation cannot support an organization-wide claim, so this Floor requirement is confirmed cooperatively, not from the curb.

signals.name: Exposed admin / database
signals.what: Whether remote-admin or database ports answer on public addresses.
signals.measure: A Level 2 determination. The curb passively observes only the one web host the domain resolves to; whether remote-admin, database or file-sharing services are reachable across the organization's public addresses is confirmed at Level 2.
signals.limit: Held to Level 2 for the same reason as B4: one host is not the infrastructure.

signals.name: DNS hygiene
signals.what: Whether the zone is signed and certificate issuance is restricted.
signals.measure: The domain is queried for a DS record (DNSSEC delegation) and for CAA records; their presence is recorded.
signals.limit: Presence is recorded, not correctness: the DNSSEC signature chain is not validated end to end, and a present CAA record is not proof that certificate issuance is constrained in practice.

signals.name: Network reputation
signals.what: Whether the web address sits on a conservative malware and attack blocklist.
signals.measure: The resolved address is joined against the FireHOL level1 aggregate.
signals.limit: Shared and CDN addresses belong to the provider, not the organization.

signals.name: US Treasury sanctions (public record)
signals.what: Whether the organization is designated on a US Treasury sanctions list.
signals.measure: The organization's exact legal name and aliases are matched against the OFAC lists in the US Consolidated Screening List. This is a matter of public-record standing, separated from technical security posture.
signals.limit: A matter of standing, not a security control, and never scored against the Floor. Name matching can produce false positives on common names; every candidate is reviewed and only exact matches are kept.

signals.name: Ransomware leak site
signals.what: Whether the organization has been posted as a victim on an extortion leak site.
signals.measure: The actor's domain is searched on ransomware.live and each result read by hand; a listing is kept only when the victim named is the actor itself. Any listing is recorded as documented exposure, dated and linked, and is not scored against the Floor.
signals.limit: A listing is the attacker's claim. Some groups recycle old data or post fabrications; the listing is shown with its date and group so it can be read as such.

changes.summary: DMARC methodology updated to RFC 9989 (obsoletes RFC 7489 and RFC 9091). The pct tag is now treated as retired and t=y as a testing flag. The measurement was corrected to separate the observed DNS record, the policy it requests, and actual receiver behaviour (which is not measured). A record requesting enforcement (p=quarantine or reject) now clears the observable Floor even in a legacy pct<100 partial rollout, which is shown as a caveat rather than counted as a failure; the earlier v0.4 model required pct=100 for a pass and mislabelled partial rollouts as not enforcing. Language that inferred receiver behaviour ('is rejected', 'not reliably rejected', 'fully enforce') and security.txt over-claims ('no reporting channel exists') were removed across the summaries, findings, tables and aggregates so every figure derives from one shared interpretation. Raw records are preserved on each profile; only the interpretation and headline framing changed.

First public draft. Two independent axes (Floor vs Standard Practice, Level 1 vs Level 2); DMARC established as the single curb-observable Floor control; sanctions and leak-site listings separated as public record, never scored against the Floor; inclusion evidence required for every organization.
